## 润色后全文

**1. Introduction**

With the rapid development of the industrial Internet of Things (IoT), an increasing number of sensors, machines, programmable logic controllers and edge devices are deployed in factories, power plants, transportation systems and many other industrial settings. These devices continuously collect data such as temperature, pressure, vibration, current and flow rate. An industrial IoT system can provide real-time monitoring and intelligent control, and it is important for improving production efficiency, reducing maintenance costs and ensuring safety. However, because industrial systems are complex and operating conditions keep changing, abnormal events are unavoidable. A sensor may drift, a valve may become blocked, a communication link may be interrupted, or a machine may develop an early fault. If such anomalies are not detected in time, they may cause production stoppages, equipment damage, environmental pollution and even personal injury. Anomaly detection for the industrial IoT has therefore become an active research topic in both academia and industry.

Traditional anomaly detection methods can be roughly divided into statistical, distance-based, density-based, clustering-based and reconstruction-based approaches. These methods have been widely used, but they are not well suited to modern industrial IoT data. First, industrial IoT data are usually high-dimensional, noisy and strongly temporally dependent. Second, sensors are not independent: they are linked by physical connections and logical correlations, and these relationships are difficult to describe with traditional vector-based methods. Third, labeled anomaly samples are scarce in real industrial settings because faults are rare and manual labeling is expensive. Fourth, industrial systems are dynamic: their topology and data distribution may change with the production plan, the season and equipment aging. These challenges mean that traditional methods often achieve unsatisfactory performance.

In recent years, deep learning has made great progress in computer vision, natural language processing and speech recognition, and many researchers have tried to apply it to anomaly detection. An autoencoder can learn normal patterns through reconstruction, a recurrent neural network can model temporal sequences, and a generative adversarial network can learn the data distribution. In some cases these deep learning methods outperform traditional ones. Most of them, however, consider each sensor or each time series separately and ignore the graph structure among sensors and devices. In the industrial IoT, the sensor network is naturally a graph: sensors are nodes, physical connections or communication links are edges, and the data collected by a sensor are its node features. A sequence model alone cannot fully exploit the spatial dependence between sensors, which is a limitation.

A graph neural network (GNN) is a deep learning model designed for graph-structured data. It aggregates information from neighboring nodes and updates node representations through message passing. GNNs can model topology and node relationships well and have been successfully applied to social network analysis, recommendation systems, traffic prediction and molecular property prediction. For industrial IoT anomaly detection, GNNs have a natural advantage: on one hand, they can capture the spatial correlation between sensors through the graph structure; on the other hand, they can be combined with temporal models to capture temporal dependence. GNN-based anomaly detection therefore has the potential to improve detection accuracy and reduce the false alarm rate.

Nevertheless, several challenges remain when GNNs are applied to industrial IoT anomaly detection. First, constructing a reasonable graph is not trivial. A graph can be built from the physical topology, the communication topology, the correlation coefficient or domain knowledge, but each choice has advantages and drawbacks. Second, industrial IoT data are temporal, whereas a simple GNN processes only a static graph and cannot model the dynamic change of the graph. Third, anomaly detection is usually unsupervised or semi-supervised because anomaly labels are scarce; the GNN must be trained without labels, and the anomaly score must be designed carefully. Fourth, industrial IoT systems have real-time requirements, so the model cannot be too complex and the inference time cannot be too long.

To address these problems, this paper proposes a GNN-based anomaly detection method for the industrial IoT, called the Temporal Graph Attention Autoencoder (TGA-AE). The main idea is to combine a temporal encoder, graph attention aggregation and a reconstruction decoder in a unified framework. Specifically, we first construct the industrial IoT graph from physical connections and data correlations. We then use a sliding window to divide the multivariate time series into sequence samples. A temporal encoder based on the gated recurrent unit extracts the temporal feature of each node, and a graph attention layer aggregates neighbor information. Finally, the decoder reconstructs the node features, and an anomaly score is computed from the reconstruction error and the prediction error. The model is trained with an unsupervised reconstruction loss and prediction loss, so it requires no anomaly labels during training.

The contributions of this paper are as follows. First, we design a graph construction method that combines the physical topology with data correlation, reflecting both the structural and data relationships of the industrial IoT. Second, we propose a temporal graph attention autoencoder that jointly models temporal and spatial dependence. Third, we design a hybrid anomaly score that combines the reconstruction error with the prediction error, improving detection performance. Fourth, we conduct experiments on several industrial IoT datasets and show that the proposed method is effective compared with baseline methods.

The rest of this paper is organized as follows. Section 2 describes the proposed method in detail. Section 3 presents the experiments and analyzes the results. Section 4 concludes the paper and discusses future work.

**2. Method**

**2.1 Problem Definition and Overall Framework**

In this paper, we consider an industrial IoT system containing N sensors or devices. The data collected by the system can be represented as a multivariate time series X = {x_1, x_2, ..., x_T}, where x_t in R^N is the observation at time step t and T is the length of the time series. At the same time, we construct a graph G = (V, E, A), where V is the node set with |V| = N, E is the edge set, and A in R^{N×N} is the adjacency matrix. Each node v_i corresponds to a sensor or device, and each edge e_{ij} represents a physical connection, communication link or data correlation between node i and node j. The feature of node i at time step t is denoted h_i^t, the observation vector of sensor i within a sliding window.

The goal of anomaly detection is to learn a scoring function f: X -> R^T that assigns an anomaly score s_t to each time step t. If s_t exceeds a threshold τ, time step t is considered anomalous. In training we use only normal data, because anomaly labels are very scarce in the industrial IoT. In testing, the anomaly score is computed by the trained model and the threshold is chosen by a given strategy.

The overall framework of TGA-AE is shown in Figure 1. Because the figure is not included in this draft, we describe it in the text. The framework has four parts: a data preprocessing module, a graph construction module, a temporal graph autoencoder module and an anomaly scoring module. The preprocessing module normalizes the raw data and divides it into sliding windows. The graph construction module builds the graph from the physical topology and correlation analysis. The temporal graph autoencoder module encodes the temporal graph data and reconstructs the input. The anomaly scoring module computes the anomaly score and makes the decision.

**2.2 Graph Construction for Industrial IoT**

Graph construction is a key step for GNN-based anomaly detection. In the industrial IoT there are two kinds of relationship between sensors. The first is physical, for example when two sensors are installed on the same machine or one sensor is upstream of another. The second is based on data, for example when two sensors are strongly correlated during normal operation. Using only the physical relationship may make the graph too sparse and fail to reflect important data correlations, whereas using only data correlation may introduce spurious edges, because correlation does not always imply causation. We therefore combine the two.

For the physical relationship, we use prior knowledge of the industrial system to build a physical graph G_p = (V, E_p, A_p). If a physical connection exists between nodes i and j, we set A_p(i,j) = 1; otherwise A_p(i,j) = 0. For the data relationship, we compute the Pearson correlation coefficient between sensors i and j on the normal training data:

ρ_{ij} = cov(x_i, x_j) / (σ_i σ_j),

where x_i and x_j are the time series of sensors i and j, cov(·,·) is the covariance, and σ_i and σ_j are the standard deviations. We then add a data edge when |ρ_{ij}| exceeds a threshold θ. The data adjacency matrix A_c is

A_c(i,j) = 1, if |ρ_{ij}| ≥ θ and i ≠ j; A_c(i,j) = 0, otherwise.

We then fuse the physical and data graphs to obtain the final graph, with fusion adjacency matrix

A = α A_p + (1 - α) A_c,

where α in [0,1] is the fusion weight. In the experiments we set α = 0.5 as the default. Edge weights are row-normalized so that each row sums to 1, which avoids scale problems in graph aggregation.

The graph in the industrial IoT is not always static. When the production plan changes or equipment ages, the correlation between sensors may change. We therefore design a dynamic graph update strategy. In training we use the whole normal training set to compute the correlations and obtain a static graph. In testing we recompute the correlations over a sliding window and update the graph every L time steps, which allows the graph to adapt to changes in operating conditions. A window that is too short makes the correlation estimate unstable, whereas a window that is too long prevents the graph from reflecting changes in time. We examine the choice of L in the experiments.

**2.3 Data Preprocessing and Sliding Window**

Raw industrial IoT data usually have different scales and contain missing values. To reduce the influence of scale, we apply z-score normalization to each sensor:

x'_{i,t} = (x_{i,t} - μ_i) / σ_i,

where μ_i and σ_i are the mean and standard deviation of sensor i in the training data. Missing values are filled by linear interpolation. If the missing ratio of a sensor is too high, we remove that sensor from the graph, because unreliable data may introduce noise into the model.

We then use a sliding window to divide the time series into samples. The window length is W and the step is S. For each time step t, the input sample is the data in the window [t-W+1, t], and the label of the sample is the anomaly label at time step t. In training we use only normal samples. In testing, each sample is fed to the model and the anomaly score at time step t is computed. The window length W should be large enough to cover the temporal pattern; if W is too large, however, the model becomes more complex and inference slower. The default setting is W = 60 and S = 1, and we also perform a sensitivity analysis in the experiments.

**2.4 Temporal Encoder**

The temporal encoder extracts the temporal feature of each node. Because industrial IoT data are time series, a recurrent neural network is a natural choice. We use the gated recurrent unit (GRU) as the temporal encoder because of its simple structure and its ability to mitigate the vanishing-gradient problem. For node i, the input sequence in the window is x_{i,t-W+1}, ..., x_{i,t}. The GRU updates its hidden state as

z_t = σ(W_z x_t + U_z h_{t-1} + b_z),
r_t = σ(W_r x_t + U_r h_{t-1} + b_r),
h_t = (1 - z_t) ⊙ h_{t-1} + z_t ⊙ tanh(W_h x_t + U_h (r_t ⊙ h_{t-1}) + b_h),

where z_t is the update gate, r_t is the reset gate, h_t is the hidden state, σ is the sigmoid function, ⊙ is element-wise multiplication, and W, U and b are trainable parameters. The hidden state h_{i,t} at the last time step is used as the temporal representation of node i. To preserve temporal information at every time step, we also use the hidden states of all time steps in the decoder. The temporal encoder is shared by all nodes, so the number of parameters does not grow with the number of nodes.

A simple GRU, however, processes each node independently and ignores the spatial relationship between nodes. We therefore add a graph attention layer after the temporal encoder. The graph attention layer aggregates information from neighboring nodes and updates node representations, thereby combining temporal and spatial features.

**2.5 Graph Attention Aggregation**

The graph attention network (GAT) is a GNN that uses an attention mechanism to aggregate neighbor information. Compared with simple graph convolution, GAT assigns different weights to different neighbors, which makes it more flexible. For node i at time step t, the input is the temporal representation h_{i,t} and the neighbor representations h_{j,t} for j in N(i). The attention coefficient is

e_{ij,t} = LeakyReLU(a^T [W h_{i,t} || W h_{j,t}]),

where W is the weight matrix, a is the attention vector, || denotes concatenation, and N(i) is the neighbor set of node i. The coefficients are normalized with softmax:

α_{ij,t} = exp(e_{ij,t}) / Σ_{k in N(i)} exp(e_{ik,t}).

The aggregated representation is

h'_{i,t} = σ(Σ_{j in N(i)} α_{ij,t} W h_{j,t}).

To stabilize training, we use multi-head attention, concatenating or averaging the outputs of K heads. We concatenate in the hidden layer and average in the output layer:

h'_{i,t} = ||_{k=1}^K σ(Σ_{j in N(i)} α_{ij,t}^k W^k h_{j,t}).

After the graph attention layer we add a residual connection and layer normalization. The residual connection mitigates the over-smoothing problem of GNNs, and layer normalization accelerates convergence. The output of the graph attention block is denoted g_{i,t}. The block can be stacked for several layers, but in the experiments two layers are enough; with too many layers, performance decreases because of over-smoothing.

**2.6 Reconstruction Decoder and Anomaly Score**

The decoder reconstructs the input from the latent representation. We use a GRU-based decoder with a fully connected layer. The latent representation g_{i,t} is fed to the decoder, and the reconstructed value is

x̂_{i,t} = W_d h^d_{i,t} + b_d,

where h^d_{i,t} is the hidden state of the decoder GRU. The reconstruction loss is the mean squared error between input and reconstruction:

L_rec = (1/(N W)) Σ_{i=1}^N Σ_{t=1}^W (x_{i,t} - x̂_{i,t})^2.

The reconstruction error alone is not sufficient for anomaly detection, because the model may reconstruct some anomaly points well when the anomaly is not obvious. We therefore add a prediction branch that uses the latent representation to predict the next time step:

x̂_{i,t+1} = W_p g_{i,t} + b_p.

The prediction loss is

L_pred = (1/(N (W-1))) Σ_{i=1}^N Σ_{t=1}^{W-1} (x_{i,t+1} - x̂_{i,t+1})^2.

The total training loss is a weighted sum of the reconstruction and prediction losses:

L = λ L_rec + (1 - λ) L_pred,

where λ in [0,1] is the weight. In the experiments we set λ = 0.7.

In testing, the anomaly score of node i at time step t is a combination of the reconstruction and prediction errors:

s_{i,t} = β (x_{i,t} - x̂_{i,t})^2 + (1 - β) (x_{i,t} - x̂_{i,t-1})^2,

where β is the weight and x̂_{i,t-1} is the prediction of time step t from the previous time step. The anomaly score of the whole system at time step t is the maximum or the average of the node scores. We use the maximum because an anomaly in one sensor may be enough to indicate a system anomaly. The system score is then smoothed by a moving average to reduce false alarms. If the smoothed score exceeds the threshold τ, the time step is detected as anomalous.

The threshold τ is selected on a validation set. Because anomaly labels are scarce, we use normal validation data to estimate the distribution of the anomaly score and set τ to μ + 3σ of the normal score, a common strategy in unsupervised anomaly detection. We also compare different threshold selection methods in the experiments.

**2.7 Training Algorithm and Complexity**

The training algorithm of TGA-AE proceeds as follows. First, we preprocess the training data and construct the graph. Second, we initialize the parameters of the temporal encoder, the graph attention layers and the decoder. Third, we sample mini-batches of sliding windows and feed them to the model. Fourth, we compute the reconstruction and prediction losses and update the parameters with the Adam optimizer. Fifth, we repeat these steps until convergence. Finally, we use the normal validation data to select the threshold.

The complexity of the model depends on the number of nodes N, the window length W, the hidden dimension d and the number of edges E. The temporal encoder has complexity O(N W d^2), the graph attention layer O(E d + N d^2), and the decoder O(N W d^2). The total complexity is therefore O(N W d^2 + E d). In the industrial IoT the number of nodes is usually moderate, so the model can be trained and inferred in reasonable time. If a system has thousands of sensors, however, graph attention may be expensive. In future work we will consider sampling-based GNNs to reduce complexity.

**3. Experiments**

**3.1 Datasets**

To evaluate the proposed method, we conduct experiments on three industrial IoT datasets: SWaT, WADI and SMD. SWaT is collected from a secure water treatment testbed and contains 51 sensors and actuators recorded over 11 days. WADI extends SWaT, contains 123 sensors and actuators, and is collected from a water distribution testbed. SMD is a server machine dataset containing 38 sensors collected from 28 servers. These datasets are widely used in anomaly detection research. Anomaly labels are provided by the datasets, but we use them only in testing; in training we use only normal data.

The statistics of the datasets are summarized in Table 1. Because the table is described in the text, we list the key information here. SWaT has 51 nodes, WADI has 123 nodes, and SMD has 38 nodes. The number of test samples and the anomaly ratio differ across datasets: the anomaly ratio is about 12% for SWaT, 5.99% for WADI and 4.16% for SMD. The data are z-score normalized, and missing values are filled by linear interpolation.

**3.2 Baselines and Metrics**

We compare the proposed method with several baselines: PCA, Isolation Forest, LSTM-AE, a GAN-based method, GraphSAGE-AE and GAT-AE. PCA is a traditional linear method that uses the reconstruction error in the principal-component subspace. Isolation Forest is a tree-based method that detects anomalies by isolation path length. LSTM-AE is a deep learning method that uses an LSTM autoencoder to reconstruct the sequence. The GAN-based method uses a generative adversarial network to learn the normal distribution. GraphSAGE-AE is a GNN-based method that uses GraphSAGE to aggregate neighbor information and an autoencoder to reconstruct the input. GAT-AE is similar to our method but does not use the temporal encoder or the prediction branch. These baselines cover traditional, deep sequence and graph-based methods, making the comparison relatively comprehensive.

The evaluation metrics are precision, recall, F1-score and AUC. Precision is the ratio of true anomalies among detected anomalies, recall is the ratio of detected anomalies among true anomalies, F1-score is their harmonic mean, and AUC is the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve. Because anomaly detection is an imbalanced problem, F1-score and AUC are more informative than accuracy. We also report the false alarm rate (FAR), the ratio of normal samples wrongly detected as anomalies, to evaluate practical usability.

**3.3 Implementation Details**

The proposed method is implemented in PyTorch. Experiments are run on a server with an NVIDIA RTX 3090 GPU and 64 GB of memory. The hidden dimension of the GRU is 64, the number of graph attention heads is 4, and the number of graph attention layers is 2. The window length W is 60, the step S is 1, and the batch size is 64. The learning rate is 0.001, and the optimizer is Adam. Training runs for 100 epochs with early stopping at a patience of 10. The fusion weight α is 0.5, the correlation threshold θ is 0.6, the loss weight λ is 0.7, and the score weight β is 0.5. These hyperparameters are selected on the validation set.

For the baselines we use the official implementation when available and otherwise implement them in PyTorch. For a fair comparison, all methods use the same data preprocessing and the same sliding window. For traditional methods the window is flattened into a vector, whereas for deep learning methods the window is fed as a sequence. Each experiment is repeated 5 times and the average result is reported.

**3.4 Overall Results**

The overall results are shown in Table 2. Because the table is not included in this draft, we describe the results in the text. On SWaT, the proposed method achieves a precision of 0.91, a recall of 0.88, an F1-score of 0.89 and an AUC of 0.95. LSTM-AE achieves an F1-score of 0.82 and an AUC of 0.89, and GAT-AE achieves an F1-score of 0.85 and an AUC of 0.91. The proposed method improves the F1-score by 7.0% over LSTM-AE and by 4.0% over GAT-AE. On WADI, the proposed method achieves an F1-score of 0.84 and an AUC of 0.92, also better than the baselines. On SMD, it achieves an F1-score of 0.86 and an AUC of 0.93. The traditional PCA and Isolation Forest methods have lower F1-scores because they cannot capture the complex temporal and spatial dependence. The GAN-based method has a good AUC but relatively low recall, because the generator may overfit the normal data and the anomaly score is unstable.

These results show that graph-based methods generally outperform non-graph methods, because industrial IoT data have strong spatial correlation that GNNs can exploit. The proposed method outperforms GAT-AE because it uses the temporal encoder and the prediction branch: the temporal encoder captures temporal dependence, and the prediction branch detects anomalies that are not well reconstructed. Combining the reconstruction and prediction errors is therefore effective.

The improvement on WADI is smaller than on SWaT, possibly because WADI has more nodes and a more complex graph, and the correlation between sensors is less stable. The graph construction method may introduce spurious edges that degrade performance. In future work we will consider causal graph construction to improve graph quality.

**3.5 Ablation Study**

To verify the effectiveness of each component, we conduct an ablation study comparing the proposed method with four variants: (1) TGA-AE without the graph attention layer (w/o GAT), (2) TGA-AE without the temporal encoder (w/o GRU), (3) TGA-AE without the prediction branch (w/o Pred), and (4) TGA-AE without the data correlation graph (w/o Data Graph). The results are shown in Table 3. Because the table is described in the text, we summarize the main findings here.

On SWaT, the w/o GAT variant has an F1-score of 0.81, 8.0% lower than the full model, showing that the graph attention layer is important for capturing spatial correlation. The w/o GRU variant has an F1-score of 0.80, 9.0% lower, indicating that the temporal encoder is necessary for industrial IoT time series. The w/o Pred variant has an F1-score of 0.85, 4.0% lower, showing that the prediction branch improves detection, especially for anomalies that are not obvious in the reconstruction. The w/o Data Graph variant has an F1-score of 0.84, 5.0% lower, meaning that the data correlation graph provides useful information beyond the physical graph.

The ablation study shows that every component contributes positively. Graph attention and the temporal encoder are the most important components, while the prediction branch and the data correlation graph also have significant effects.

**3.6 Parameter Sensitivity**

We also analyze the sensitivity of several key hyperparameters: the window length W, the fusion weight α, the correlation threshold θ and the loss weight λ. The results are shown in Figure 2. Because the figure is not included in this draft, we describe the trends in the text.

As W increases from 20 to 60, the F1-score increases, and it decreases slightly when W exceeds 60. A short window cannot cover enough of the temporal pattern, whereas a long window may introduce noise and increase model complexity. W = 60 is therefore a good choice.

The best performance for the fusion weight α is around 0.5. When α is too small, the graph is dominated by data correlation and the physical relationship is ignored; when α is too large, the graph is dominated by the physical topology and data correlation is ignored. Fusing the two kinds of relationship is beneficial.

The F1-score is stable when the correlation threshold θ is in the range 0.5 to 0.7. If θ is too small, many spurious edges are added; if θ is too large, the graph becomes too sparse. θ = 0.6 is therefore a reasonable setting.

For the loss weight λ, the best performance is obtained at λ = 0.7. This means the reconstruction loss is more important than the prediction loss, but the prediction loss still contributes, consistent with the ablation study.

**3.7 Robustness and Efficiency Analysis**

In real industrial IoT, data often contain noise and missing values. We therefore test the robustness of the proposed method under different noise levels, adding Gaussian noise with standard deviations of 0.01, 0.05 and 0.1 to the test data. The F1-score of the proposed method decreases from 0.89 to 0.86, 0.82 and 0.76, respectively, while GAT-AE decreases from 0.85 to 0.80, 0.74 and 0.66. The proposed method is more robust because the temporal encoder and the prediction branch mitigate the influence of noise. At very high noise levels, however, the performance of all methods decreases substantially, which remains a challenge.

We also compare the inference time of different methods. On SWaT, the proposed method takes about 12 ms per sample, while LSTM-AE takes about 8 ms and GAT-AE takes about 10 ms. The proposed method is slightly slower because it includes the temporal encoder, graph attention and prediction branch, but the inference time is still acceptable for real-time industrial monitoring, since industrial sensors usually sample at the second or minute level. If a system requires millisecond-level response, the model must be further optimized or compressed.

**3.8 Discussion**

The experimental results show that the proposed method is effective for industrial IoT anomaly detection, but it has several limitations. First, graph construction depends on prior knowledge and the correlation threshold; without accurate prior knowledge, the physical graph cannot be constructed accurately. Second, the dynamic graph update strategy is simple and may not capture sudden changes in topology. Third, the model is trained in an unsupervised way and the anomaly-score threshold is selected from normal validation data; if that data are not representative, the threshold may be suboptimal. Fourth, the experiments use public datasets, whereas real industrial deployment is more complex: concept drift, sensor failure and communication delay are not fully considered.

In future work we will pursue four directions. First, we will study causal graph construction to reduce spurious edges. Second, we will design an adaptive graph update mechanism based on online learning. Third, we will combine semi-supervised and active learning to exploit the limited anomaly labels. Fourth, we will deploy the method on edge devices and optimize the model for real-time industrial applications.

**4. Conclusion**

In this paper we propose a GNN-based anomaly detection method for the industrial IoT called the Temporal Graph Attention Autoencoder (TGA-AE). The method combines a temporal encoder, graph attention aggregation and a reconstruction decoder in a unified framework. We construct the industrial IoT graph from the physical topology and data correlation, use a GRU to extract temporal features and graph attention to aggregate neighbor information, and then use the decoder to reconstruct the input and a prediction branch to predict the next time step. The anomaly score is computed from the reconstruction and prediction errors, and the threshold is selected from normal validation data. The model is trained with an unsupervised loss, so it requires no anomaly labels during training.

We conduct experiments on the SWaT, WADI and SMD datasets. The results show that the proposed method achieves better F1-scores and AUCs than the baselines, including PCA, Isolation Forest, LSTM-AE, the GAN-based method, GraphSAGE-AE and GAT-AE. The ablation study shows that graph attention, the temporal encoder, the prediction branch and the data correlation graph all contribute positively. The parameter sensitivity analysis gives reasonable hyperparameter settings, and the robustness analysis shows that the method has a degree of noise resistance.

The paper also has limitations. Graph construction is not fully automatic, and the dynamic graph update is simple. Model complexity is relatively high for large-scale industrial IoT systems. Real deployment and concept drift are not fully studied. In future work we will improve graph construction through causal discovery, design an adaptive graph update method, and deploy the model on edge devices. We believe that graph neural networks have great potential for industrial IoT anomaly detection, and we hope this work provides a useful reference for related research.
